IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00754

The Kahanes' exceptionally close examination reveals similarities and correspondences between the doctrines, episodes and vocabulary of the Corpus Hermeticum and those of Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival. This immediately raises the question of historical transmission. How could knowledge of Hermeticism have reached Wolfram? The course of the Hermetic initiate's life and that of Parsifal agree so closely that, in the scholars' view, direct knowledge alone can explain the resemblance—and can also unlock Wolfram's allusions to his “sources.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00755

The authors distinguish three stages. (a) First, the preservation of Greek Hermetic material in Syriac and Arabic literature. (b) Next, the survival and further development of the Arabic- and Persian-language Hermetic tradition within medieval Islamic civilisation. Here a leading role clearly belongs to the Sabians of Harran (ancient Carrhae, in Mesopotamia), who survived within the Islamic world until the eleventh century, though not without difficulty.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00756

They never wholly succeeded in being recognised among the Ahl al-Kitâb, the communities possessing a scripture revealed by a prophet, despite having their own “Book” and their own “prophets,” Hermes and Agathodaimon. Their devotion to Hermes, their astral liturgies, their teaching on Light and Darkness—the affinities with Suhrawardi's teaching deserve fuller treatment than we have so far been able to give them—and their particular familiarity with the fourth treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum, entitled “The Mixing Bowl,” all help us place this community in its spiritual setting.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00757

Thabit ibn Qurra, a distinguished ninth-century scientist and philosopher, founded a new branch of Sabianism in Baghdad and wrote, among other works, a book on the “Liturgical Institutions of Hermes.” We also know that a very large number of Arabic treatises attributed to Hermes remain unpublished.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00758
(c) Finally, we must consider the transmission to the West of this Greek-Arabic Hermetic material.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00759

From this point the inquiry turns first to identifying the name by which the Corpus Hermeticum designates the Grail, then to tracing the people who carried the tradition westward, and finally to answering the question: what should we understand by the Urparzival, the supposed “original” Parsifal?
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00760

The central idea is this: the mysterious krater, or mixing bowl, which gives the fourth treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum its title, is none other than the Grail, both in meaning and in the very history of the word.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00761

“God filled a great mixing bowl with intellect and sent it down to earth. He appointed a herald and commanded him to proclaim to the hearts of men: Immerse yourself in this bowl, you who are able, you who believe you will rise again to the One who sent the bowl to earth, you who know why you came into being. All those, then, who heeded the proclamation and were baptised with this baptism of intellect shared in knowledge (gnosis), and became perfect human beings, because they had received intellect.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00762

We shall meet the theme of the messenger from beyond in Suhrawardi's initiation stories. The herald invites all who are capable of understanding the bowl's purpose to enter the baptism it offers. Human beings thus fall into two groups, according to whether they possess the intelligence—and with it the awareness of divine mystery—that makes this possible: those whom spiritual knowledge transforms into “perfect human beings,” and those who will never know why they came into this world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00763

To connect this with Wolfram's text, let us follow the clues our scholars have identified. The Greek word κρατήρ (kratēr, a mixing bowl) is, they argue, the same word as graal, already used by Chrétien de Troyes in a form based on the Latin. The Greek became Latin crater and cratera; the development into gradale and graal—words for a cup, dish, vessel or basin—presents, in their account, no difficulty.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00764

We leave the details of their philological argument to the authors and turn instead to the astral meaning of the vessel. An ancient tradition imagined two bowls traced among the stars, one holding wisdom and the other forgetfulness. Before entering earthly bodies, souls bathe in or drink from one or the other. The theme already appears in Macrobius (fourth–fifth century) and in the well-known Coptic Gnostic book Pistis Sophia.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00765

Now, in Book IX of Parzival, at the heart of the poem and the culmination of Parsifal's instruction by the hermit, we read that Flegetanis—the learned “pagan,” descended from Solomon, who first wrote the history of the Grail—“discovered, while studying the constellations, profound mysteries of which he spoke only with trembling. There was, he said, an object called the Grail. He had clearly read its name in the stars. A host of angels had brought it down to earth and then flown away, far beyond the stars. Those angels were too pure to remain here below.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00766

The mixing bowl and the Grail are therefore, in their symbolic pattern, “something” brought from Heaven to Earth. Following his “sources” and the tradition known to Macrobius, Wolfram derives the name not from an earthly vessel but from a constellation, which the Kahanes identify as the constellation Crater. The Holy Grail is associated with that constellation as a vas mysticum, a mystical vessel.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00767
We shall also encounter the Grail as a mystical bowl or cup in the Iranian tradition.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00768

But does that conflict with the image of the Grail as a stone, which appears elsewhere in Wolfram's Parzival? Here again the Kahanes seem to us to have offered a sound solution to a problem often treated as an insoluble riddle. At the close of the Hermetic treatise on the Mixing Bowl comes a comparison whose crucial image is the “magnetic stone” (magnētis lithos): “This, then, O Tat, is the image of God that I have drawn for you as best I can.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00769

“If you contemplate it carefully and picture it with the eyes of your heart, believe me, my child, you will find the way to the things above. Or rather, the image itself will show you the way. For contemplation has a power of its own: it takes hold of those who have once contemplated, and draws them to itself, just as, they say, the magnetic stone draws iron to itself.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00770

Wolfram seems almost to paraphrase this final exhortation when he says that “by the power of this stone the phoenix burns and turns to ashes; yet out of the ashes life is born again. Through this stone the phoenix sheds its old nature and returns in all its splendour, as beautiful as ever.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00771

Wolfram continues: “No man is so ill that, if brought into the presence of this stone, he is not certain to escape death for the whole week following the day on which he saw it. Whoever sees it ceases to grow old [...]. This stone gives a man such strength that his bones and flesh immediately regain their youth. This stone is also called the Grail.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00772

We shall suggest later that the ascent of Hermes, as Suhrawardi knows and understands it, brings together the magnetic stone of the Corpus Hermeticum and the image of the phoenix. We are therefore inclined to agree with the Kahanes that Wolfram uses the stone as another name for the Grail.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00773

Of course, this is not a claim that a physical utensil is literally a stone. It is an image, and precisely one that preserves the relationship established in the Corpus Hermeticum between the magnetic stone and the mixing-bowl Grail. In other words, Wolfram's word “stone” tells us nothing about the Grail's physical shape, substance or use. “Nothing indicates that the Grail is not a vessel.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00774

In any case, the stone serves as the receptacle for the mystical host placed upon it every Good Friday by the “heavenly dove.” What we can read in this image is that “the soul, symbolised by the phoenix, is drawn to the Monad, or Grail, symbolised by the magnetic stone; the soul's purification and regeneration are symbolised by the phoenix's death in fire and rebirth.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00775

Following this line of thought, the Kahanes believe they can decipher the strange expression lapsit exillis, proposing that it should be read as lapis exilis, the “humble” or “insignificant stone.” Wolfram writes: “All that sustains them”—the Grail's Templars—“comes from a precious stone which in its essence is perfect purity. If you do not know it, I will tell you its name: it is called lapsit exillis.” These lines have prompted endless debate.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00776

But the Kahanes point out that the magnetic stone is commonly described—for example, by Claudian in the fourth or fifth century—as decolor, obscurus, vilis: colourless, dark and of little worth. A thirteenth-century text calls it an “ugly black stone.” The magnetic stone is thus indeed a lapis exilis; yet because it is magnetic, it is also something altogether different from what its humble appearance suggests. A few lines earlier, Wolfram called it a “precious stone.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00777

For our part, we would suggest looking, at least by way of symbolic comparison, toward the Black Stone of Shiite Islamic gnosis—the Stone set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba. A long tradition attributed to the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, tells how it was originally an angel of Paradise, Adam's angelic companion, whom God “cast” down to earth to accompany Adam into exile. At first Adam does not recognise it beneath its meagre, dark, mineral appearance (lapis exilis).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00778
But when his eyes are opened, he understands, and the Stone becomes the cornerstone of the pure spiritual Temple. We can only point to this theme here, without pursuing it further.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00779

As for Wolfram's “sources,” he names them, but in a fashion that has unleashed almost as many speculations as the Grail itself. Three names in particular have caused serious difficulties for interpreters: Trevrizent, the wise hermit who initiates Parsifal into the mystery of the Grail; Flegetanis, the “pagan” sage who first wrote the history of the Grail; and Kyot the Provençal, who supposedly brought it to Wolfram. Together they form a formidable puzzle. The Kahanes' research seems to us, for the first time, to offer a coherent way through it.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00780

Take Trevrizent first. Once again, we can only summarise the conclusions, not retrace every step of the argument. Wolfram describes Trevrizent as a holy ascetic, a teacher and a sage. He is an exemplary initiate of the “Mixing Bowl.” All his distinguishing features match the spiritual portrait of Hermes: the guide who initiates the Grail brotherhood has the same characteristics as Hermes, guide of the Hermetic brotherhood.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00781

In Wolfram, Trevrizent plays the role Hermes plays in the Corpus Hermeticum (Treatises III, IV and XIII), initiating Parsifal into the knowledge of the stars with the authority of Hermes, founder of astrological science. What, then, lies behind his curious name, distorted like so many names of Latin origin in Wolfram's poem? Here the Kahanes had a fortunate insight that casts a sudden light upon the way forward.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00782

By a chain of careful philological deductions, they propose that Trevrizent conceals the Old French Trible Escient—“threefold wisdom,” or “threefold knowledge.” Trevrizent, the sage of threefold wisdom, would then be none other than the Hermes of the entire Hermetic tradition: in Latin, triplex sapientia vel triplex scientia; in Arabic, as Suhrawardi's commentators also know, mothalleth bi'l-hikmat. This Arabic expression translates the Greek Trismegistos, “thrice-great,” the epithet that makes Hermes Trismegistus the “Hermes of Hermes.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00783

Yet Hermes is not only a teacher and initiator. He is also the supposed author of the Hermetic treatises, the sage whose knowledge embraces the whole range of learning: the natural world, the stars and the invisible worlds.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00784

And it is in these two capacities, the Kahanes argue, that Hermes appears in Wolfram: as Trevrizent, the sage of threefold wisdom, and as Flegetanis. The latter name has so far resisted every attempt at explanation. That should not surprise us when we recall the extraordinary changes Greek names underwent in being written in Arabic and then transcribed back into Latin, especially in alchemical texts (Hippocrates becoming Picatrix, Empedocles becoming Pandolfus, and so on). It seems plausible that the beginning of the name preserves something like Arabic falak, “celestial sphere” or “heaven.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00785

More importantly, the Kahanes have assembled a cluster of traits that allow them to compare Hermes as portrayed in Arabic sources—particularly his expertise in astrology and its associated sciences—with Wolfram's Flegetanis, who explains how the Grail came to earth. Among the Arabic works attributed to Hermes was a major treatise on astronomy, al-falakîyat al-kobrâ. Our scholars suggest that falakîyat may help explain the name Flegetanis.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00786

Admittedly, something remains unresolved in this explanation, and its completion may have to come through Persian. Whatever the final answer, the Kahanes make a perceptive observation. In Islamic teachings about the prophets, Hermes is identified with Enoch, who is himself identified with Idris. Wolfram, meanwhile, describes Flegetanis as a pagan through his father, a Jew through his mother, and a descendant of Solomon. Such a double ancestry could well reflect the merging of Hermes and Enoch into a single figure.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00787

Wolfram also has Flegetanis insist that anyone who hopes to see the Grail must be baptised—a demand entirely consistent with baptism in the Hermetic “Mixing Bowl.” All this suggests that Trevrizent and Flegetanis may conceal two aspects of the same Hermes: Trevrizent, the sage of threefold knowledge, is Hermes the initiator; Flegetanis is Hermes the author of the Hermetic treatises.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00788

If we accept both identifications, one problem remains: how the Arabic Hermetic material reached the West, and who transmitted it to Wolfram. This brings us to the third name, Kyot the Provençal. The debate seems hopeless so long as we assume that Kyot gave Wolfram a complete Urparzival—an already composed, fully told story of Parsifal—for no trace survives of such a work in Provençal. Here again I can only refer to the evidence by which the Kahanes identify Kyot the Provençal with William of Tudela, a contemporary of Wolfram (Kyot being Guillot, a Catalan-Aragonese diminutive of William).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00789

William was a Jewish convert whose native language was then so close to Provençal that he could reasonably be called, on linguistic grounds, “Kyot (Guillot) the Provençal.” He knew Latin, Hebrew and Arabic, and understood the abc—in Arabic, the abjad, the philosophical alphabet and the mystical science of letters. He was skilled in astrological geomancy, a practice whose symbolism was then regarded as part of theology itself. The astrological passages in Wolfram's Parzival, which clearly display a direct familiarity with Arabic terminology, have precisely this character: their chief concern is less with any particular event in the sky than with its symbolic meaning and the interpretation it demands.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00790

We cannot linger further over the Kahanes' fine book, though we hope that the brevity of our account has not diminished the force of its argument. Their comparative table sets out a striking series of correspondences between the stages of Hermetic initiation and the journey of Wolfram's initiate, embodied by Parsifal. This is not merely a novel of education (Erziehungsroman), but a poem of initiation. The same mystical vessel—the mixing-bowl Grail—stands at the centre of both the fourth treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum and Wolfram's Parzival.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00791

The Monad in the Hermetic text and the Grail in Wolfram are alike the beginning and root of all things. “Nothing exists without a beginning. As for the beginning itself, it arose from nothing but itself, since it is the beginning of everything else. Being the beginning, therefore, the Monad contains every number without itself being contained in any of them.” The procession of the Grail—twenty-four maidens appearing in succession and carrying seventeen lights between them, until the Grail queen appears—is thus “a representation of the soul's mystical journey toward the Monad, itself symbolised by the Grail.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00792

How, then, should we imagine the Urparzival? Kyot-Guillot found the original version of the story Wolfram tells in Tudela (previously read as Toledo), “written in pagan script”—that is, in Arabic. The details of its origin remain mysterious.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00793

But according to Wolfram's own testimony, Kyot-Guillot gave him access to it. What he provided, however, was not a finished book, an already coherent and complete tale that Wolfram needed only to copy out. Wolfram himself says that he worked with no model before him—“without a book.” The Hermetic elements he used are scattered throughout the whole body of Hermetic writings.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00794

The Kahanes therefore propose that the Urparzival was the body of teachings and symbols gathered by Kyot-Guillot and Wolfram, which Wolfram himself then shaped into the story of an initiate: the story of Parsifal.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00795

It seems to us that the Hermetic elements in Suhrawardi's work point to a similar process. (Let us recall once more the tradition that traces the origins of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, to the sister of Hermes.) Elsewhere we have translated the passage in which Suhrawardi describes Hermes' ecstatic ascent. Like the account of Hermes' vision of his Perfect Nature, this story bears the marks of an Arabic-language Hermetic tradition that may have anticipated the initiate's journey as Suhrawardi would later shape it in his own stories of initiation.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00796

Hermes prays at night in the Temple of Light: he is gathered into himself, in the presence of the “sun” of his soul, hidden within the material body. When “the column of dawn burst forth, he saw a land sinking away”—his physical being consumed, like the phoenix, in the fire of “Eastern” Light as his soul blazes beyond the boundaries of the body, kindled by the Light of Lights. Hermes cries out to his “father” for help: the Nous, his agathos daimôn, or Perfect Nature.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00797

The reply comes: “Take the ray of light as your rope; grasp it and climb to the battlements of the Throne.” Hermes is carried up to Heaven, like Enoch, with whom Islamic teachings about the prophets identify him, or like Elijah in his chariot of fire. The ray of light that he grasps as a rope, drawing him upward toward the “battlements of the Throne,” plays the role of the magnetic stone, the Grail, in Wolfram.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00798

We know that, for “Eastern” theosophy, the bursting forth of dawn is the appearance, in the mystical “East,” of the splendour of the Light of Glory, the Xvarnah. For the initiate, the return to this “East” is the morning of his glorification. At the coming of that morning—or that spring—we shall encounter Suhrawardi's mysterious bird, the Simorgh. Insofar as we can identify the Simorgh with the phoenix, we see in Suhrawardi the return of the phoenix image evoked by Wolfram.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00799

But the fire here is mystical: it is the soul becoming incandescent in “Eastern” Light, the light of the Xvarnah or the Grail. If, during the early Middle Ages, certain people of Harran or even of India, inspired by the story of Hermes, gave themselves to actual flames, that was one of the tragedies of taking the literal meaning (sensus litteralis) literally.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00800

Hermes' ascent is his arrival at the source of Light and Life—the source reached by Suhrawardi's initiate on the mystical Sinai, at the Emerald Rock (Mount Qaf, Mount Salvat), at the end of the Tale of the Western Exile. For the shaykh al-Ishrâq, it is the same event in the world of the Malakût, the spiritual realm, as the ecstasies of Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster, who are carried into the presence of the “sources of the Light of Glory” (Xvarnah).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00801

Dawn breaking forth, the soul rising in the “East” on the horizon of the world of pure Light—this is precisely what the vision of the Xvarnah means to Suhrawardi. (The connection between dawn and the Xvarnah is already marked in the Avesta by the name “mountain of dawns.”) The “Eastern” hero is transferred into the mystical world of Hurqalya. He becomes hidden from this world while still alive, as Kay Khosraw did, as the Twelfth Imam of the Shiites did, and as the Holy Grail itself now is.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00802

Whether we say that Parsifal takes the Holy Grail back to the East, or that Galahad carries it to Sarras, from where it is taken up to Heaven, the event these images express is the same, as we shall have occasion to say again. For “East” and “Sarras,” like Hurqalya, are places in the “eighth clime,” invisible to the senses of those who have not been “baptised in the Mixing Bowl.” This passage into another realm is the initiate's transfiguration, anticipating what will be fulfilled at the end of his own spiritual destiny. Suhrawardi will express it in a magnificent “Grail story” with Kay Khosraw as its hero (see below, § 5).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00803

Thus, on one side, the research we have just examined takes us from the Holy Grail of Wolfram's Parzival back to Hermeticism. We find a corresponding witness to the purpose of Hermetic gnosis in Suhrawardi's account of Hermes' ascent, whose mystical meaning he understands to be the same as that of the visions of Kay Khosraw and the prophet Zoroaster.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00804

All are heroes of the spiritual epic that leads them back to the “East”: to the splendour of Light, to Ishrâq, which the ancient Persians called the Xvarnah. And now, on the other side, the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, will lead us back to the Holy Grail, if we follow the second investigation announced earlier. The circle closes—a circle whose centre and circumference are both Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy,” as can happen with spiritual circles, unlike those of the physical world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00805

This second investigation, as we have said, is the work of a Zoroastrian scholar, Sir Jahangir C. Coyajee, and dates from some thirty years ago. Unfortunately, he knew nothing of the work of the shaykh al-Ishrâq, which at the time was still unpublished.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00806

Yet if Coyajee's proposed link between the Xvarnah and the Holy Grail, and between Kay Khosraw's Iranian knighthood and the knights of the Grail, proves plausible, then the appearance of the heroes of Iranian epic in Suhrawardi's mystical tales gives that link, to our mind, an entirely different kind of evidence. In those tales, heroic action is fulfilled as a spiritual epic. The earlier study followed traces within the texts themselves from Wolfram back to Arabic-language Hermeticism. The path from Xvarnah to Grail, unfortunately, offers no equally precise signposts.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00807

Yet we already know that Suhrawardi crossed this distance effortlessly: within his own work it lies between the vision of the Xvarnah granted to Kay Khosraw and the “Grail story” whose hero is Kay Khosraw. From Suhrawardi onward, at any rate, the connection is made, and its effects reach backward into the entire past. That is why we speak of evidence “of another order”: the evidence of spiritual events that make up the soul's history, always present, breaking through the one-way passage of time. Such evidence is not simply a conjecture drawn from reconstructing the fading material traces of a vanished past.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00808

The connecting link through which Coyajee suggests that Iranian knighthood met the knighthood of the Grail is not Hermeticism but another religion: Mithraism. In fact, these two initiatory traditions had already influenced one another before the time of those we call the “Platonists of Persia.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00809

We can outline the problem Coyajee sets himself, following his account as faithfully as possible. Much ingenuity and effort have gone into explaining the legend of the Holy Grail—through the cult of Adonis, the Eleusinian mysteries, those of Samothrace, and so forth. By drawing attention to Iranian parallels, however, Coyajee proposes a hypothesis that could explain several otherwise puzzling features.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00810

As he reminds us, it has remained difficult to explain how the theme and legend of the Grail in their Christian form became linked with the whole Celtic cycle that includes the Grail motif, the saga of King Arthur and the knights of the Round Table. Some have attributed the connection to Robert de Boron; others believe that he found it already established in an earlier Latin source; still others credit Chrétien de Troyes. In the German cycle represented by Wolfram's work, another event enters the picture—the very one that led the first study we examined toward Hermeticism.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00811

According to Coyajee, the Iranian parallels ultimately form a body of clues suggesting that the Grail cycle contains elements derived from the Iranian epic tradition. Above all, they would allow us to recognise one underlying image in the Holy Grail and the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory. The idea of the Xvarnah is organically bound to that of a company of knights gathered around a line of people who bear its power.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00812

We encountered the same theme in Suhrawardi, inspired by sayings of the First Imam of Shiism. Prominent among these bearers is Kay Khosraw, a central figure for Suhrawardi because he gives his name to the Khosrawânîyûn, the “Eastern” sages or theosophers, the ishrâqîyûn. Coyajee will compare Kay Khosraw with Parsifal and King Arthur.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00813

But if we are seeking an actual historical route by which these traditions met, we must find some material trace of contact between the Celtic and Iranian worlds. Coyajee believes that, on the Iranian side, the contact came through the religion of Mithra: Mithraism.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00814

There is, first, the special link established by the hymns of the Avesta between Mithra and the Xvarnah (see the Zamyad Yasht and the Mihr Yasht). Wherever the worship of Mithra appears, reverence for the Xvarnah accompanies it. As we have recalled, Xvarnah means both Glory and Destiny; the Greek translation of “royal Xvarnah” was Tykhê Basileos, the king's fortune or destiny.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00815

Consider, too, the details of Mithraic imagery: the vessels, dishes and mixing bowls shown in sculptures of Mithra slaying the bull, calling to mind the rites of his mysteries and Mithraic communion feasts. Mithra himself appears as a young figure armed with sword and spear; on coins from Bactria, the Xvarnah is represented as a god carrying a spear. Bowl, sword, spear: all are characteristic objects in Grail literature.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00816

Second, Coyajee finds a common ideal linking Mithraic fellowship to the brotherhood of the Grail: the quest for the Source of Life, moral and physical purity, and the close bond between companions. Perhaps Mithraism has too often been described as a religion of “soldiers.” It was not so much that professional soldiers were especially drawn to it; rather, initiates themselves received the title miles or milites, “soldier” or “soldiers,” by virtue of their initiation. That is not quite the same thing.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00817

And it is worth noting that in medieval Latin miles means precisely “knight.” The bond of brotherhood is formed in the service of a cause that invites comparison between the Iranian tradition underlying Mithraism and the chivalry of the Round Table. There is certainly much to reflect upon here. Unfortunately, so much has been destroyed that we shall never know more than a little about Mithraic rites and initiation. We have referred several times to the document known as the “Liturgy of Mithras.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00818

Yet what matters most is the direction of the mystical journey held out by each tradition. The initiate of Mithra was introduced to the soul's journey toward the Islands of Light, across the ocean of stars and beyond the planetary spheres.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00819

Perhaps the paths that lead our knights to Avalon or Sarras converge there too, as do those leading to the Green Island, the dwelling place of the Twelfth Imam, or to the “Western Paradise” of Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light in Japanese Pure Land Buddhism. For in every case we are concerned with the “world of Hurqalya,” the “eighth clime,” and that intermediate “East” itself still lies to the west of the “greater East” of the Jabarût, the higher world of divine powers.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00820

Let us return from these distant realms and glance at our maps—on which, of course, the cities of the “eighth clime” cannot appear. There is nevertheless an interesting geographical question: where might the Mithraic priesthood and the Celtic priesthood have met? Coyajee recalls the enormous spread of Mithraism through Gaul, Italy, Britain and Roman Germany. Remains of mithraea, temples dedicated to Mithra, have been found in great numbers.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00821

Conversely, Druidism can be spoken of as extending from Ireland to Asia Minor, in Galatia. And in Asia Minor itself, communities of Magi had been established since the Achaemenid period. We have already had occasion to recall the connection between those Magi and the worship of Mithra. A meeting of Iranian and Celtic traditions, of Magi and Druids, thus seems more than plausible. Mithraic traditions may have entered Celtic beliefs long before the rise of the Roman Empire.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00822
Certainly, there is no objection in principle to this broad picture.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00823

Yet without texts, plausibility cannot rise to the certainty possible when a teaching has been explicitly set down. Here scholarship can do little more than identify analogies. Its position is less favourable than in the case of Wolfram and Hermeticism, where the texts themselves can be closely compared. For our purposes, then, it seems better to remain faithful to the phenomenological approach to the end: to seek above all to understand what shows itself to Suhrawardi, and how and why it shows itself to him in precisely that way.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00824

We must begin with the spiritual event—an event that has truly taken place, but has taken place spiritually: his vision and his decisive commitment, in which the visions of Hermes and Zoroaster, the Light of Glory and the Holy Grail, come together.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00825

From this starting point we must seek to understand the secret—the bâtin, the inner meaning—that he reveals to us, and how and why he reveals it. This is why we have preferred not to speak here of the migration of symbols, the history of ideas, great historical “currents,” or the recurring archetypes of the unconscious. Such explanations are all acceptable, provided one accepts the more or less agnostic assumption that the only interesting and knowable thing is, so to speak, the “gesture” made by a thinker or a doctrine—not what that gesture is actually trying to show us.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00826

But what Suhrawardi is trying to show us is the direction of Ishrâq, of the Malakût, the spiritual world. It is there that all the events of importance to the “Oriental” philosophy of divine wisdom take place—the events whose heroes are Hermes, Kay Khosraw, and Zoroaster. The Malakût belongs neither to the past nor to the future. It is neither something that has been left behind nor something that “still remains to be done.” In itself it is Present, with an absolute presence: a presence freed from every condition we impose when we define something as past or future.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00827

Can we bring this world into view by pursuing phenomenology to its ultimate conclusion? This “unveiling of what is hidden” (kashf al-mahjûb) is precisely what Suhrawardi and his companions accomplish when they show us what they see: an “Orient” that appears on none of our maps, where the deeds of heroes continue and reach their fulfilment as a mystical epic, and where Iranian chivalry and the chivalry of the Grail thereby meet. Once Suhrawardi, the shaykh al-Ishrâq, has taught us how to make this “orientation” a reality, the parallels identified by Mr Coyajee—particularly those concerning the Xvarnah and Kay Khosraw—can begin to bear fruit.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail

2. The Forms of Manifestation and the Lineage of the Xvarnah and the Holy Grail
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00828

Here again, we can touch on only a few of the many comparisons proposed by the Zoroastrian scholar, and only in broad outline. At the same time, we shall indicate what we believe is the direction these comparisons must take if observations about the forms in which the Xvarnah and the Grail appear, and about the sacred lineages of those who possess or guard them, are to become genuinely meaningful.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00829
As has rightly been observed, neither the Xvarnah nor the Holy Grail is described as possessing any single, fixed form.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00830
Yet both appear in similar forms, from which certain shared qualities emerge. The Holy Grail, we are told, was “neither of wood, nor of metal, nor of stone, nor of horn, nor of bone.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00831

Nevertheless, it could take on material appearances—a vessel, a cup, a bowl, a stone—alongside the other “Wondrous Objects,” the lance and the sword. The Xvarnah, too, is spiritual in its essence: so much so that it is, before anything else, the object of a struggle between heavenly powers and the opposing forces of Ahriman.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00832
But it, too, can appear as a cup, a stone, a lance, a flame, even a bird (when it deserts King Yima), or a stretch of sea (when it escapes Afrasyab the Turanian).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00833

In the Iranian epic tradition, one form in which the Xvarnah became “material” was a stone: a talisman, a sacred object charged with supernatural power. Kay Khosraw had inherited it from his distant ancestors. It possessed extraordinary healing powers: it could restore reason to the deranged and bring the dead back to life. (We have already seen that the Xvarnah is also the energy that holds a being's existence together—its “light” and its “destiny.”) This talisman bestowed courage and all the qualities of the spiritual strength that ensures victory.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00834

Likewise, in Wolfram von Eschenbach's epic, the Stone “which is also called the Grail,” brought down from heaven by angels and entrusted to the guardianship of a mystical order of knights, grants those who contemplate it long life, even immortality, because the Grail is the source of Life.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00835

The form of the cup is no less celebrated. We need only recall the central object of the Christian Grail cycle. Identified with the chalice of the Last Supper, entrusted to Joseph of Arimathea, who had collected Christ's blood in it, the holy Vessel is brought to the White Island—that is, Great Britain—by a company of mysterious messengers. Their leader varies with the version of the story: in Robert de Boron's account it is Bron, Joseph of Arimathea's brother-in-law, who becomes the first king of the sacred Lineage; in the prose Lancelot, for example, it is Joseph's son Josephé, the mystical figure of the first and only Christian bishop.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00836

In either case, the journey is not one whose route and stages we could plot on a map. It is a passage of an altogether different order. The supernatural powers of this cup, and the many themes of the “quest for the Grail,” fill the whole body of Grail literature. One can only wish that the complete “canon of Grail writings” might someday be assembled in a single edition, in a modern language accessible to any willing reader.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00837

The cup is also one of the forms in which the Xvarnah manifests itself. In the Iranian epic cycle it is called the Jâm-gîtî-nemâ, “the cup (the Grail) that reveals the universe,” or the “mirror of the universe.” At the spring equinox the whole cosmos can be contemplated within it—not so much the affairs of the “seven climes” of the earthly world as those of an invisible world, of which the planets and constellations are merely signs.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00838

But to attain this vision one must be a consecrated figure, a hieratic person such as Kay Khosraw, invested with the royal Xvarnah. The poem by Suhrawardi that we shall examine later, with Kay Khosraw as its hero, is among the finest expressions of the mystical meaning of this Iranian Grail. The cup became a recurring theme throughout Persian mystical literature: the Jâm-e Jam, the Grail of Jamshid.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00839

The lance and the sword provide further parallels. Armed with the supernatural lance, Kay Khosraw attacks the magician's evil fortress. The lance strikes the wall; the dark stronghold vanishes; the demons occupying it scatter. In its place a different castle appears, splendid and bathed in light and flowers.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00840

By this deed Kay Khosraw reveals himself as bearer of the Xvarnah and successor to Kay Kâûs. He is “the one who knows the meaning of the lance.” Likewise, it is only when Parsifal finally asks about the meaning of the lance and the Grail that the spell is broken—the magical prohibition that had held nature in desolation, barrenness, and deprivation. Once more the earth comes alive with the brilliance of flowers and the songs of birds.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00841

But the Iranian epic, like our Grail cycle, also knows the knight who fails: Fariborz. “He in whose hand the sword breaks” is the image of a knight whose quest ends in defeat. As for the “castle of the Grail,” Kay Khosraw's story will allow us to return to it shortly.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00842

To sum up, very broadly: in both traditions there is a mysterious virtue or power which manifests itself through a Wondrous Object—a talisman or sacred instrument—surrounded by an aura of holiness like the most sacred relic. Whether the object is a form of the Xvarnah or the Grail itself, it offers the nourishment of immortality and the illumination of knowledge.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00843

Whoever possesses the Xvarnah in its fullness possesses not only the gifts associated with spiritual consecration but also the victorious strength of the knight. The Xvarnah passes from one hero to the next without any visible intermediary. This is what leads Mr Coyajee to compare the royal succession of those who bear the Xvarnah with the lineage of the guardians of the Grail.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00844

Just as the Grail is brought to earth by angels and entrusted to knights who are the purest of men, so the Xvarnah originates among the powers of Light. It belongs at first to Ohrmazd, to his archangels, to the Yazatas, and to all beings of light, both those of the invisible spiritual world (mênôk) and those of the material earthly world (gêtîk). It passes from sovereign to sovereign through the first two legendary dynasties of the Iranian epic: the Pishdadians (the “lawgivers”) and the Kayanids, from Kay Qobad to Kay Khosraw.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00845

It passes to Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, prophet of the religion of Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda, the “Lord-Wisdom”), and to King Vishtaspa, his protector. It passes to Zoroaster's last son, who is to be born at the end of our Aeon: a Zarathustra redivivus, a Zoroaster returned—the final Saoshyant, whose relationship to Zoroaster is analogous to that of the Twelfth Imam to the Prophet Muhammad. The Light of Glory “will accompany the victorious Saoshyant and his friends when he makes a new world, free from old age, death, and decay; eternally living, eternally growing.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00846

We should notice that this vision of the last things, characteristic of Iranian spirituality as a whole, necessarily entails the present concealment of the Xvarnah. It entails the present concealment of the Twelfth Imam in the same way, just as it entails the concealment of the Grail. Here, where these ideas meet, we might find what all those whom Suhrawardi calls the Khosrawanians (Khosrawâniyûn) have in common with the chivalry of the Grail. We might also find the foundation of a shared ethic, through which both groups devote themselves, incognito, to the same struggle. For each, their strength remains sacred and invincible so long as their hidden identity is preserved.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00847

The struggle for the Xvarnah “began in Heaven.” The Holy Spirit of Ohrmazd (Spenta Mainyu) and Ahriman (Angra Mainyu) contend for it (Yasht XIX, 46). The sacred history of the Xvarnah on earth is the manifestation and continuation, in the visible material world, of the struggle between Ohrmazd's powers of Light and Ahriman's opposing powers of Darkness. From this perspective, too, we ought to consider what the Iranian dynasty of the Kayanids may have in common with the dynasty of the Grail's guardians.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00848

But we have the impression that Mr Coyajee, as a comparative historian, intends to go much further. (It is strange that, on the shifting ground of material facts and surviving remains, the critical historian is willing to venture much further than the phenomenologist, whereas the phenomenologist is the one who ventures forward as soon as the task is to acknowledge spiritual facts as spiritual facts and establish their standing.) The Zoroastrian scholar identifies parallels that allow him to set the old King Kay Kâûs beside Titurel; Kay Kâûs's son Siyavakhsh beside Amfortas, the “wounded king”; and Kay Khosraw beside Parsifal.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00849

The aged Kay Kâûs longs for the arrival of the hero of his line—his grandson—to whom the Xvarnah will pass. Because his son Siyavakhsh has been killed on the orders of the king of Turan, the land of Iran lies desolate and devastated. A heavenly voice tells the Iranians that if they wish this ruin and desolation to end, they must set out to seek the future bearer of the Xvarnah. When Kay Khosraw succeeds in killing the evil Turanian, the land of Iran bursts into flower again, just as the domain of the Grail does upon Parsifal's return.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00850
Thus, according to our author, an Iranian royal line would correspond to the Grail lineage of the German cycle.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00851

Yet, as we know, the lineage of the Grail's guardians is not the same in Wolfram's account—the German cycle—as it is, for example, in Robert de Boron's Joseph and the cycle that grew out of it. This has given rise to no shortage of difficulties and debate.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00852

We shall consider only the aspect that interests Mr Coyajee. Joseph of Arimathea prays that guardianship of the Grail may remain with his descendants. Are these descendants to be understood as a family line by blood, or as a succession of mystical initiates? Now, the Zamyad-Yasht (the hymn to the Dea terrestris, the goddess of the earth) describes how the Xvarnah became attached to, and passed in succession through, eight kings in a line beginning with Kavi Kavata (Kay Qobad) and ending with Kavi Husravah (Kay Khosraw). This is the line of the Kayanids as later told in Ferdowsi's Shâh-Nâmeh. Other texts, meanwhile, make it possible to identify eight guardians of the Grail between Joseph of Arimathea and King Pelles.
